nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
In python x is True and x == True have exactly the same semantics, because True and False are global singletons. Generally, having two different operators that do the same thing in the your IR is not desirable because it means passes have to reason about both cases if they want to optimize the pattern. Additionally, optimizations like Common Subexpression Elimination will no trigger.
@torch.jit.script
def foo(x: bool):
    return x == True, x == True

torch._C._jit_pass_cse(foo.graph)
torch._C._jit_pass_dce(foo.graph)
print(foo.graph)

Will give a graph with a single aten::eq node, where as the semantically equivalent
@torch.jit.script
def foo(x: bool):
    return x  is True, x == True

torch._C._jit_pass_cse(foo.graph)
torch._C._jit_pass_dce(foo.graph)
print(foo.graph)

Will have two different comparison nodes. This is of particular interest because we have optimizations that optimize through aten::eq nodes like: #55926 and #55978, which are being used in Symbolic Shape Analysis.
We already have an existing pass that runs whenever we emit IR to do similar normalization, we could add this pattern there. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/csrc/jit/passes/normalize_ops.cpp

nodes.bodyText:
Originally raised in #50937 (comment)
The COO to CSR tensor conversion is implemented in

  
    
      pytorch/torch/_tensor.py
    
    
        Lines 928 to 940
      in
      3a777b6
    
  
  
    

        
          
           if self.is_sparse: 
        

        
          
               coalesced_self = self.coalesce() 
        

        
          
               row_indices = coalesced_self.indices()[0] 
        

        
          
               ro = [0] 
        

        
          
               i = 0 
        

        
          
               for irow in range(self.shape[0]): 
        

        
          
                   while i < row_indices.size()[0] and row_indices[i] == irow: 
        

        
          
                       i += 1 
        

        
          
                   ro.append(i) 
        

        
          
            
        

        
          
               return torch.sparse_csr_tensor(torch.tensor(ro, dtype=row_indices.dtype), 
        

        
          
                                              coalesced_self.indices()[1], coalesced_self.values(), 
        

        
          
                                              size=coalesced_self.shape, dtype=coalesced_self.dtype) 
        
    
  


and it consists of two time-consuming parts:

coalescing if the COO tensor is uncoaleasced
row indices compression procedure

Indeed, taking a coalesced COO sample with size=(1000, 1000) and nnz=500, about 1.5% of the to_sparse_csr call time is spend in coalescing and 98% of the time in running the row indices compression loop.
The slowness of the row indices compression loop has two origins:

it is implemented in Python
it uses a suboptimal algorithm

Indeed, a sample of row indices with size[0] == 1000 and nnz=500, a pure Python algorithm in
https://github.com/pearu/gcs/blob/b54ba0cba9c853b797274ef26b6c42386f2cafa3/gcs/storage.py#L24-L45
is about 3x faster than used in to_sparse_csr, and when applying numba.njit to the compress_indices function, about 83x speedup is achieved compared to to_sparse_csr.
The performance of COO to CSR tensor conversion can be improved by implementing a more efficient row indices compression algorithm (see compress_indices referenced above) in C++.
cc @VitalyFedyunin @ngimel @aocsa @nikitaved @pearu @mruberry

🐛 Bug
A pytorch module passed through prepare_qat_fx is no longer picklable, due to _PartialWrapper.
This prevents usage of the ddp_spawn accelerator.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
I modified this tutorial example to run prepare_qat_fx and try to pickle it.
pytorch==1.8.1
import torch
import pickle

from torch.quantization import get_default_qconfig
from torch.quantization.quantize_fx import prepare_qat_fx

class TwoLayerNet(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, D_in, H, D_out):
        """
        In the constructor we instantiate two nn.Linear modules and assign them as
        member variables.
        """
        super(TwoLayerNet, self).__init__()
        self.linear1 = torch.nn.Linear(D_in, H)
        self.linear2 = torch.nn.Linear(H, D_out)

    def forward(self, x):
        """
        In the forward function we accept a Tensor of input data and we must return
        a Tensor of output data. We can use Modules defined in the constructor as
        well as arbitrary operators on Tensors.
        """
        h_relu = self.linear1(x).clamp(min=0)
        y_pred = self.linear2(h_relu)
        return y_pred


# N is batch size; D_in is input dimension;
# H is hidden dimension; D_out is output dimension.
N, D_in, H, D_out = 64, 1000, 100, 10

# Create random Tensors to hold inputs and outputs
x = torch.randn(N, D_in)
y = torch.randn(N, D_out)

# Construct our model by instantiating the class defined above
model = TwoLayerNet(D_in, H, D_out)

# Try to pickle quantized model
qconfig = get_default_qconfig("qnnpack")
qconfig_dict = {"": qconfig}

model = prepare_qat_fx(model, qconfig_dict)

pickle.dumps(model)
Running this file results in:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "torch_test.py", line 45, in <module>
    pickle.dumps(model)
AttributeError: Can't pickle local object '_with_args.<locals>._PartialWrapper'

Expected behavior
Empty output; pickle.dumps should succeed

I used pytorch to predict some diseases from ecg data. (medical, 1 dimentional time series data)
Different hospitals have different lengths of ecg data because of various ecg recording machines. Instead of cropping or padding, I decided to use intact waves while doing a project.
So I used custom batch sampler to deal with this kind of data. I think this can be applied a lot in other data structure, so I made this 'issue'. What do you guys think?

🐛 Bug
In one of my scripts, I noticed that the output of torch.matmul differs depending on whether the variables are located CPU or CUDA.
The bug appears only using cuda 11.1, with cuda 10.2 it's fine.
To Reproduce
To reproduce the error, just run the following example:
import numpy as np

📚 Documentation
Issue Description
at::TensorIteratorConfig requires one to add first all outputs and only then all inputs
Wrong and will throw a confusing internal error in TensorIterator.cpp:
auto iter = at::TensorIteratorConfig()
    .add_input(input1).add_input(input2).add_input(input3)
    .add_output(output1).add_output(output2)
    .build();

Correct:
auto iter = at::TensorIteratorConfig()
    .add_output(output1).add_output(output2)
    .add_input(input1).add_input(input2).add_input(input3)
    .build();

This behavior, however, is not documented.
Suggestions

Add to the documentation in TensorIterator.h (at the top or before TensorIteratorConfig::add_output/add_input) the clause, that outputs have to be specified before inputs.
and/or
Enhance the error message in 
  
    
      pytorch/aten/src/ATen/TensorIterator.cpp
    
    
         Line 22
      in
      6032ea0
    
  
  
    

        
          
           TORCH_INTERNAL_ASSERT(num_inputs_ == 0); 
        
    
  

 to indicate that outputs have to be added before inputs.

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
The ability to pass size overides to certain dimensions when creating new tensors using the "_like" functions. For example...
input_tensor = torch.ones(2, 3, 32, 32)
new_tensor = torch.zeros_like(input_tensor, overides=[(1, N)]) 
# new_tensor shape is (2, N, 32, 32)

Motivation
I find the current situation a bit clunky as the new size N may be either smaller or larger than the current size of the target dimension leading to this....
new_tensor = torch.zeros_like(input_tensor.narrow(1, 0, 1).expand(-1, N, -1, -1))

This is worse when supporting tensors with an arbitrary number of trailing dimensions as you cannot make use of the expand function...
sizes = list(input_tensor.shape)
sizes[1] = N
new_tensor = torch.zeros(sizes, dtype=input_tensor.dtype, device=input_tensor.device)

Pitch
Adding the above mentioned "overides" keyword argument into the "_like" tensor creation operations would, in my opinion, make the above situation much more fluent to write aswell as easier to read.
Alternatives
See above examples, Im happy to hear if theres an easier way to acheive this functionality with the existing API.
Additional context
N/A
cc @gchanan @mruberry

Issue description
Size of a CSR tensor must be of length 2.  This is one of the invariance for the CSR layout, currently there are no checks for this case and size property for CSR tensors accepts len(size) > 2. See the following example:
Code example
When using the current master:
>>> import torch 
>>> crow_indices = [0, 2, 4]
>>> col_indices = [0, 1, 0, 1]
>>> values = [1, 2, 3, 4]
>>> sparse = torch.sparse_csr_tensor(torch.tensor(crow_indices),
                                                      torch.tensor(col_indices),
                                                      torch.tensor(values),
                                                      size=(2, 10, 2))
tensor(crow_indices=tensor([0, 2, 4]),
       col_indices=tensor([0, 1, 0, 1]),
       values=tensor([1, 2, 3, 4]), size=(2, 10, 2), nnz=4,
       layout=torch.sparse_csr)
>>> sparse.to_dense()
tensor([[[1, 0],
         [2, 0],
         ... 
         [0, 0]],

        [[3, 0],
         ...
         [0, 0]]])


Note:
The issue was mentioned here #56744 (comment).
CSR invariants
CSR Invariants about sizes:

Issue #57211


len(size) == 2


Checks between line 64-80: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/native/sparse/SparseCsrTensor.cpp


(crow_indices.dim == col_indices.dim == values.dim) == 1
len(crow_indices) == size[0] + 1
len(col_indices) == len(values) == nnz

CSR Invariants about values

Check 
  
    
      pytorch/aten/src/ATen/native/sparse/SparseCsrTensor.cpp
    
    
         Line 60
      in
      46a32e0
    
  
  
    

        
          
           TORCH_CHECK( 
        
    
  




crow_indices[0] == 0


Issue #56856


col_indices[crow_indices[i]:crow_indices[i+1]]
values[crow_indices[i]:crow_indices[i+1]]
crow_indices[-1] == nnz

cc @aocsa @nikitaved @pearu @mruberry

🐛 Bug
Using torch.autograd.profiler within a RPC callback function results in a couple of different behaviors that are confusing:

Fails to execute a print statement within the callback
Does not produce a profiler output file
Does not raise an error
I've also seen runs hang in certain setups that use a profiler in the callback function though I was not able to reproduce it in this small example.

Thank you @rohan-varma for helping me with this issue and suggesting using a wait() before profiling.
Related resource that I used along with Rohan's help to profile async RPCs:  https://pytorch.org/tutorials/recipes/distributed_rpc_profiling.html

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Bug
One of the recommendations to improve performance when using rpc_async/rpc_sync was to use torch.jit.script to trace the function that was being run remotely. However this results in an error since we cannot trace RRefs and all function inputs are expected to be of type Tensor.
How should one go about this? The only way to get a handle on the remote object is to pass the reference as once of the arguments to the rpc_async/rpc_sync calls.
To Reproduce
run the gist below with --use_torch_script flag
https://gist.github.com/anj-s/b2a68d7985dc7ebd8a6d95d7e7094170
Stack Trace:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "playground/herring/repro/repro_rpc_torch_script.py", line 12, in <module>
    class Server(object):
  File "playground/herring/repro/repro_rpc_torch_script.py", line 20, in Server
    def val(myobj_rref):
  File "/private/home/anj/.conda/envs/test_clone/lib/python3.8/site-packages/torch/jit/_script.py", line 1094, in script
    fn = torch._C._jit_script_compile(
RuntimeError:
'Tensor (inferred)' object has no attribute or method 'local_value'.:
  File "playground/herring/repro/repro_rpc_torch_script.py", line 21
    @torch.jit.script
    def val(myobj_rref):
        self = myobj_rref.local_value()
               ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ <--- HERE
        fut = torch.futures.Future()
        fut.set_result(self.value)

Expected behavior
Recommendation for how we should use torch.jit.script with RRefs + remote functions. Specifically how can we get a handle on the remote object if we don't pass it as an argument to the function.

🐛 Bug
The following functions unfold1 and unfold2 are expected to work the same:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F


def unfold1(x, chunk_size):
    hop_size = chunk_size // 2
    x = x.transpose(1, 2)
    x = x.unfold(-1, chunk_size, hop_size)
    return x


def unfold2(x, chunk_size):
    hop_size = chunk_size // 2
    x = x.transpose(1, 2)
    B, C, T = x.shape
    x = x.reshape(B, C, T // hop_size, hop_size)
    x = torch.cat((x[:, :, :-1], x[:, :, 1:]), dim=-1)
    return x


if __name__ == '__main__':
    device = 'cuda'
    x = torch.arange(24).reshape(2, 6, 2).float().to(device)

🐛 Bug
When installing either the current nightly or version 1.8.1 using pip/conda the tensorcore acceleration of nn.Conv3D with Nvidia GPUs is not working. However, when compiling pytorch from source it works as intended and gives a ~3x speedup relative to regular fp32 training. Given that compiling from source is something not all users will be able to do (or want to do) it would be nice if that was fixed in the pip/conda installer.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

run the following python script on different GPUs and pytorch versions
the output of the script (stdout) is two numbers representing s/iter for mixed precision and fp32, respectively. So if the output is (0.2, 0.5) then mixed precision took 0.2s whereas fp32 took 0.5s/iter. Lower is better

from time import time
from torch import nn
import torch
from torch.backends import cudnn
import numpy as np
from torch.cuda.amp import GradScaler, autocast


def run_timed_iterations_fp32(n_steps, batch, gt, loss, optimizer, model, n_warmup):
    for n in range(n_warmup):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        out = model(batch)
        l = loss(out, gt)
        l.backward()
        optimizer.step()

    times = []
    for n in range(n_steps):
        st = time()

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        out = model(batch)
        l = loss(out, gt)
        l.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        times.append(time() - st)
    return np.mean(times)


def run_timed_iterations_fp16(n_steps, batch, gt, loss, optimizer, model, n_warmup):
    scaler = GradScaler()

    for n in range(n_warmup):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        with autocast():
            out = model(batch)
            l = loss(out, gt)
        scaler.scale(l).backward()
        scaler.step(optimizer)
        scaler.update()

    times = []
    for n in range(n_steps):
        st = time()

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        with autocast():
            out = model(batch)
            l = loss(out, gt)
        scaler.scale(l).backward()
        scaler.step(optimizer)
        scaler.update()
        times.append(time() - st)
    return np.mean(times)


class VGG3D(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

        self.conv1 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(3, 32, 3, 1, 1, bias=False),
                                   nn.BatchNorm3d(32),
                                   nn.ReLU(True))
        self.conv2 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(32, 32, 3, 1, 1, bias=False),
                                   nn.BatchNorm3d(32),
                                   nn.ReLU(True))

        self.conv3 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(32, 64, 3, 2, 1, bias=False),
                                   nn.BatchNorm3d(64),
                                   nn.ReLU(True))
        self.conv4 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(64, 64, 3, 1, 1, bias=False),
                                   nn.BatchNorm3d(64),
                                   nn.ReLU(True))

        self.conv5 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(64, 128, 3, 2, 1, bias=False),
                                   nn.BatchNorm3d(128),
                                   nn.ReLU(True))
        self.conv6 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(128, 128, 3, 1, 1, bias=False),
                                   nn.BatchNorm3d(128),
                                   nn.ReLU(True))
        self.conv7 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(128, 128, 3, 1, 1, bias=False),
                                   nn.BatchNorm3d(128),
                                   nn.ReLU(True))

        self.conv8 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(128, 256, 3, 2, 1, bias=False),
                                   nn.BatchNorm3d(256),
                                   nn.ReLU(True))
        self.conv9 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(256, 256, 3, 1, 1, bias=False),
                                   nn.BatchNorm3d(256),
                                   nn.ReLU(True))
        self.conv10 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(256, 256, 3, 1, 1, bias=False),
                                   nn.BatchNorm3d(256),
                                   nn.ReLU(True))

        self.conv11 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(256, 512, 3, 2, 1, bias=False),
                                    nn.BatchNorm3d(512),
                                    nn.ReLU(True))
        self.conv12 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(512, 512, 3, 1, 1, bias=False),
                                    nn.BatchNorm3d(512),
                                    nn.ReLU(True))
        self.conv13 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(512, 512, 3, 1, 1, bias=False),
                                    nn.BatchNorm3d(512),
                                    nn.ReLU(True))

        self.conv14 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(512, 512, 3, 2, 1, bias=False),
                                    nn.BatchNorm3d(512),
                                    nn.ReLU(True))
        self.conv15 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(512, 512, 3, 1, 1, bias=False),
                                    nn.BatchNorm3d(512),
                                    nn.ReLU(True))
        self.conv16 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv3d(512, 512, 3, 1, 1, bias=False),
                                    nn.BatchNorm3d(512),
                                    nn.ReLU(True))

        self.gap = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool3d(output_size=1)
        self.classifier = nn.Conv3d(512, 10, 1, 1, 0, bias=True)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.conv1(x)
        x = self.conv2(x)
        x = self.conv3(x)
        x = self.conv4(x)
        x = self.conv5(x)
        x = self.conv6(x)
        x = self.conv7(x)
        x = self.conv8(x)
        x = self.conv9(x)
        x = self.conv10(x)
        x = self.conv11(x)
        x = self.conv12(x)
        x = self.conv13(x)
        x = self.conv14(x)
        x = self.conv15(x)
        x = self.conv16(x)
        x = self.gap(x)
        out = self.classifier(x).squeeze()
        return out


if __name__ == '__main__':
    net = VGG3D().cuda()
    data = torch.rand((4, 3, 128, 128, 128)).cuda()
    gt = torch.randint(10, (4, )).cuda()

    loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

    cudnn.benchmark = True
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()

    optim = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), 0.01)

    ret16 = run_timed_iterations_fp16(50, data, gt, loss, optim, net, 10)
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    ret32 = run_timed_iterations_fp32(50, data, gt, loss, optim, net, 10)
    print(ret16, ret32)
Expected behavior
fp16/mixed precision should be ~3x faster than fp32. This number comes from my own experiments using pytorch version that I compiled myself. I tested both Turing and Ampere GPUs. Here are my results:

pytorch 1.7.1 + cuDNN 8.1.0.77; compiled myself
3090: 0.18401368618011474 0.5708892440795899
2080ti: 0.2557570123672485 0.6653153610229492
pytorch 1.8.1 + cuDNN 8.2.0.53; compiled myself
3090: 0.1797804880142212 0.5501960325241089
2080ti: 0.21456592559814452 0.7236361074447631
pytorch '1.9.0.dev20210427+cu111' + cuDNN "8005"; installed with pip
3090: 0.685448751449585 0.7036943531036377
2080ti: 0.9805365180969239 0.7098741006851196

As you can see, both pytorch 1.7.1 + cuDNN 8.1.0.77 and pytorch 1.8.1 + cuDNN 8.2.0.53 have the expected speedup when using mixed precision. pytorch '1.9.0.dev20210427+cu111' + cuDNN "8005" does not.
(I do not have a pytorch version that I compiled myself with cuDNN 8005 but I used to have it and I know that it worked with Turing at least)
Environment
(this is the RTX 3090 system.If you need info for the RTX 2080ti system as well let me know)

nodes.bodyText:
IMHO there is a discrepancy between the docs and code of nn.Linear, when it comes to initialization.
documentation says that the weights are initialized from
uniform ( 1/sqrt(in_ feaures) , 1/sqrt(in_ feaures)):

  
    
      pytorch/torch/nn/modules/linear.py
    
    
        Lines 53 to 56
      in
      0df5740
    
  
  
    

        
          
                   weight: the learnable weights of the module of shape 
        

        
          
                       :math:`(\text{out\_features}, \text{in\_features})`. The values are 
        

        
          
                       initialized from :math:`\mathcal{U}(-\sqrt{k}, \sqrt{k})`, where 
        

        
          
                       :math:`k = \frac{1}{\text{in\_features}}` 
        
    
  


code says that the weights are initialized from
kaiming_uniform

  
    
      pytorch/torch/nn/modules/linear.py
    
    
        Lines 88 to 89
      in
      77721ee
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def reset_parameters(self) -> None: 
        

        
          
               init.kaiming_uniform_(self.weight, a=math.sqrt(5)) 
        
    
  


and that includes factors of sqrt(3), gain based on 'a', and 'fan':

  
    
      pytorch/torch/nn/init.py
    
    
        Lines 390 to 395
      in
      77721ee
    
  
  
    

        
          
           fan = _calculate_correct_fan(tensor, mode) 
        

        
          
           gain = calculate_gain(nonlinearity, a) 
        

        
          
           std = gain / math.sqrt(fan) 
        

        
          
           bound = math.sqrt(3.0) * std  # Calculate uniform bounds from standard deviation 
        

        
          
           with torch.no_grad(): 
        

        
          
               return tensor.uniform_(-bound, bound) 
        
    
  


Is that an error or am I missing something?
cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @bdhirsh @jbschlosser @anjali411 @brianjo @mruberry @albanD

🚀 Feature
Add map-style Datapipe to support new DataLoader.
Motivation
From the RFC #49440, you can find lots of issues with the previous DataLoader. So, we are working on a new design of DataLoader to support several features such as multithreading, and to prevent OOM. To support the new design of DataLoader, we have proposed the IterDataPipe for the iter-style DataPipe. But, in terms backward-compatibility,
a list of functional MapDataPipe is also needed for users. The difference between iter-style and map-style can be found here

You can take reference from the implementation of iter-style DataPipe
Note

path: torch/utils/data/datapipes/map/...
__len__ is required for map-style
__getitem__ is required for map-style
Make sure DataPipe lazy-init and loading data lazily
Make sure DataPipe is pickleable

List

 ConcatMapDataPipe
 ZipMapDataPipe
 BatchMapDataPipe
 UnbatchMapDataPipe (Likely do not want it)
 MapMapDataPipe
 UnZipMapDataPipe (Likely do not want it)
 ShuffleMapDataPipe
 FilterMapDataPipe (Likely do not want it)
 ForkMapDataPipe
 DemuxMapDataPipe (Likely do not want it, length not known in advance)
 MultiplexerMapDataPipe (Likely do not want it since the functionality doesn't make sense in Map-style? Open to suggestion if there is an actual use case)
 ...

Here are the complete list of IterDataPipe, some of which we may want to create Map-style version:

To avoid implementing every single feature twice (one in Iter-style, one in Map-style), our current guidance is that users should use the built-in IterDataPipe for various functionalities, and convert it to MapDataPipe as needed using IterToMapConverter or .to_map_datapipe(). For that reason, I don't think we will need additional MapDataPipe for now.
Feedback and suggestions are welcome here.
cc @ssnl @VitalyFedyunin @ejguan @NivekT

# idx = torch.tensor([3, 0]) # Works.

print(torch.unique(idx))

v = torch.tensor(-2.5122, requires_grad=True, dtype=torch.double)

def fn(v):
    return t.index_fill(0, idx, v)

torch.autograd.gradcheck(fn, (v,))
torch.autograd.gradgradcheck(fn, (v,))
Reason: 
  
    
      pytorch/tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml
    
    
        Lines 607 to 610
      in
      6de11c2
    
  
  
    

        
          
           - name: index_fill_.int_Tensor(Tensor(a!) self, int dim, Tensor index, Tensor value) -> Tensor(a!) 
        

        
          
             self: grad.clone().index_fill_(dim, index, 0) 
        

        
          
             value: grad.index_select(dim, index).sum() 
        

        
          
             index: non_differentiable 
        
    
  


Formula for value doesn't consider this. And thus we get the failures.
Quick Fix (tested locally):
--- a/tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml
+++ b/tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml
@@ -606,7 +606,7 @@
 
 - name: index_fill_.int_Tensor(Tensor(a!) self, int dim, Tensor index, Tensor value) -> Tensor(a!)
   self: grad.clone().index_fill_(dim, index, 0)
-  value: grad.index_select(dim, index).sum()
+  value: grad.index_select(dim, std::get<0>(at::_unique(index))).sum()
   index: non_differentiable
 
 - name: index_put_(Tensor(a!) self, Tensor?[] indices, Tensor values, bool accumulate=False) -> Tensor(a!)
Questions to tackle for fixing

Should forward error out if there are duplicate indices (my guess is this behaviour wasn't intentional) (BC breaking)?
If we decide to keep forward as is and update the backward, there would be a perf-hit. (Is it ok to have perf hit for this niche case)

🚀 Feature
Convolution ops now support batch_size=0 (#12013). We'd like to let convolution ops support inputs/weights with channel=0.
Motivation
We've encountered such a situation in detection research (facebookresearch/detectron2#2975), where the #channels is dynamically generated per iteration (and could be 0). We have to workaround it with matmul instead:
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F

C = 8
D = 16  # Cout
K = 10


def f1(features, weights, bias):
    features = features.reshape(N, C, K)
    weights = weights.reshape(N, D, C)
    bias = bias.reshape(N, D, 1)
    out = torch.einsum("nck,ndc->ndk", features, weights) + bias
    return out.reshape(1, N * D, K)


def f2(features, weights, bias):
    return F.conv1d(features, weights, bias, stride=1, padding=0, groups=N)


for N in [3, 0]:
    features = torch.rand(1, N * C, K)
    weights = torch.rand(N * D, C, 1)
    bias = torch.rand(N * D)
    out1 = f1(features, weights, bias)
    out2 = f2(features, weights, bias)
    print(torch.abs(out1.reshape(out2.shape)-out2).max())
In the above code, f2 and f1 are equivalent except that f2 crashes when N=0. The goal is to make them truly equivalent.
cc @albanD @mruberry @jbschlosser

nodes.bodyText:
Issue description
The efficient conversion between COO and CSR formats is important because constructing a sparse tensor is simplest when using COO format while many linear algebra operations involving matrix multiplications are considerably more efficient when using CSR format.
In theory, conversion between (2D coalesced) COO and CSR formats involves only the compression or decompression of row indices which are roughly O(nnz) operations while the column indices and element values are unchanged.
In pytorch, however, the conversion is complicated by the following constraints:

COO indices must have dtype torch.int64.
CSR crow_indices/col_indices can have dtype either torch.int32 or torch.int64. The support for torch.int32 is introduced to CSR to take advantage of (the most) efficient MKL matmul implementation that uses int32 indices (pytorch supports MKL LP64 only).

Namely, when one wants to use MKL support for matmul, the most optimal dtype for crow_indices/col_indices would be int32. However, the conversion between the COO and CSR formats becomes more expensive because of the forced int32-int64 casting of both row and column indices.
The inefficiency of this is seen in #56392 (comment) and #56392 (comment) where several methods for sampling CSR and COO tensors are benchmarked (CPU only):

sampling a CSR tensor directly is about 4-9x more performant than sampling a COO tensor
sampling a CSR tensor from a COO tensor sample via to_sparse_csr method is about 60-280x slower than sampling a CSR tensor directly

Discussion
Considering the low complexity of compression operation and the point 1 and 2, the slow-down factor of 60-280x from a COO->CSR conversion is too high, IMHO, and is likely caused by the int32-int64 casting operations and intermediate copies of tensors.
There appears to be no good dtype choice when a user application requires the usage of MKL for efficient matmul operations and conversions between the COO and CSR formats, at the same time. Unless:

int32 indices support is implemented for COO format
pytorch will support MKL ILP64 that allows using int64 indices in MKL routines
more coding effort will be put to optimize coo.to_sparse_csr (and unimplemented csr.to_sparse) to take into account int32-int64 casting requirements.

The last option seems most doable but has the least potential to improve the COO-CSR conversion performance.
Any thoughts?
cc @aocsa @nikitaved @pearu @mruberry @gchanan
nodes.title: Inefficient conversion between COO and CSR formats

🐛 Bug
I get a segmentation fault during the backward step with a standard 3D U-Net on the CPU with large images (tensor size >= (1,1,360,360,360)).
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Save the below code as a script and run on a machine with at least 120 GB of free RAM and in an environment with just PyTorch (and dependencies) installed.

`
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import faulthandler

class Layer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self,inputs,outputs):

        super(Layer, self).__init__()

        k = 3
        p = (k-1)//2
        s = 1

        self.layer = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv3d(inputs,outputs,kernel_size=k,padding=p,stride=s),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv3d(outputs,outputs,kernel_size=k,padding=p,stride=s),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True)
        )

    def forward(self,x):
        return self.layer(x)

class UNet(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self):

        super(UNet, self).__init__()

        self.encoding_layers = nn.ModuleList()
        self.encoding_layers.append(Layer(1,32))
        self.encoding_layers.append(Layer(32,64))
        self.encoding_layers.append(Layer(64,128))
        self.encoding_layers.append(Layer(128,256))

        self.decoding_layers = nn.ModuleList()
        self.decoding_layers.append(Layer(256,128))
        self.decoding_layers.append(Layer(128,64))
        self.decoding_layers.append(Layer(64,32))

        self.downsamples = nn.ModuleList()
        self.downsamples.append(nn.MaxPool3d(2))
        self.downsamples.append(nn.MaxPool3d(2))
        self.downsamples.append(nn.MaxPool3d(2))

        self.upsamples = nn.ModuleList()
        self.upsamples.append(nn.ConvTranspose3d(256,128,kernel_size=2,stride=2))
        self.upsamples.append(nn.ConvTranspose3d(128,64,kernel_size=2,stride=2))
        self.upsamples.append(nn.ConvTranspose3d(64,32,kernel_size=2,stride=2))

        self.map_to_output = nn.Conv3d(32,3,kernel_size=1,stride=1)

    def forward(self,x):

        x1 = self.encoding_layers[0](x)
        x2 = self.encoding_layers[1](self.downsamples[0](x1))
        x3 = self.encoding_layers[2](self.downsamples[1](x2))
        x = self.encoding_layers[3](self.downsamples[2](x3))

        x = self.upsamples[0](x)
        x = self.decoding_layers[0](torch.cat([x3,x],axis=1))

        x = self.upsamples[1](x)
        x = self.decoding_layers[1](torch.cat([x2,x],axis=1))

        x = self.upsamples[2](x)
        x = self.decoding_layers[2](torch.cat([x1,x],axis=1))

        return self.map_to_output(x)

def main():

    faulthandler.enable()

    model = UNet()

    for L in [32, 64, 128, 256, 400]:

        x = torch.rand(1,1,L,L,L)
        print(f'input shape: {x.shape}')

        out = model(x)
        print(f'output shape: {out.shape}')

        out.sum().backward()
        print(f'Finished for L = {L}')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

`

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
I would love to see an implementation of the incomplete Cholesky factorization.
Motivation
The incomplete Cholesky factorization has proved useful in a wide number of ML problems, especially those related to optimization (Nocedal and Wright, 2006). It's particularly useful as a preconditioner for iterative algorithms like conjugate gradient and Lanczos.
LAPACK's potrf returns incomplete factorizations; however, at the moment there is no way to access them in pytorch, since a runtime error is raised when info != 0. Even when cholesky is called as torch.cholesky(A, out=L), the result does not populate into buffer L.
Pitch
Perhaps it would make sense to follow scipy's schematic. Like pytorch, scipy's public-facing cholesky routines (linalg.cholesky and linalg.cho_factor) wrap potrf and raise an error when info != 0. However, they also provide a means to call LAPACK directly via linalg.get_lapack_funcs. This gives added control to more advanced LAPACK users. Pytorch has a number of routines that call LAPACK directly, such as orgqr and geqrf, and perhaps it be possible to add one more for potrf.
Alternatively, another idea is to let the partial factorization populate into the buffer L when cholesky is called as torch.cholesky(A, out=L). This might require some additional documentation about derivatives etc for the case of an incomplete factorization.
cc @jianyuh @nikitaved @pearu @mruberry @heitorschueroff @walterddr @IvanYashchuk @xwang233

nodes.bodyText:
Issue description
As in title.
Code example
When using the current master:
>>> import torch
>>> t = torch.tensor([[0, 1, 0], [2, 0, 3]])
>>> t.to_sparse()
tensor(indices=tensor([[0, 1, 1],
                       [1, 0, 2]]),
       values=tensor([1, 2, 3]),
       size=(2, 3), nnz=3, layout=torch.sparse_coo)
>>> t.to_sparse_csr()
tensor(crow_indices=tensor([0, 1, 3]),
       col_indices=tensor([1, 0, 2]),
       values=tensor([1, 2, 3]), size=(2, 3), nnz=3)

Notice that the CSR tensor str output does not include layout value.
The issue is also related to #56685 .
Discussion
Following COO tensor convention, the expected result would be:
>>> t.to_sparse_csr()
tensor(crow_indices=tensor([0, 1, 3]),
       col_indices=tensor([1, 0, 2]),
       values=tensor([1, 2, 3]),
       size=(2, 3), nnz=3, layout=torch.sparse_csr)

One might argue that the layout output is superfluous in the COO tensor str output:

no layout is reported in strided tensor str output
the layout is obvious from the output content: COO has indices/values, CSR has crow_indices/col_indices/values properties.

However, as witnessed in the case of COO and CSR tensors, some properties are shared (e.g. values) in between different layouts. Hence, there is a risk that the tensor layout (of some format to be introduced in future) cannot be derived from the str output. So, I would recommend always include the layout property in tensor str output, except for the strided tensor case (due to BC). What do you think?
cc @aocsa @nikitaved @pearu @mruberry

The kineto-dependency configuration does not use standard cmake facilities to find include and library for CUPTI but instead hardcodes a few paths. This means that as soon as the file location differs from what is hardcoded, finding cupti fails. This can happen when CUPTI is actually present and is even detected by the general cuda dependency.
(For obscure reason I have arch triples in the library path and CUPTI is in my CMAKE_INCLUDE_PATH but not in the location where the PyTorch Kineto build-configuration looks.)
Also, it seems that there may be cases where the kineto checks fail to override a .so that is found but a .a would be nicer (but I'm not exactly sure about it).
The culprit

      e97c17a
    
  
  
    

        
          
               if(EXISTS ${CUDA_SOURCE_DIR}/extras/CUPTI/lib64/libcupti_static.a) 
        

        
          
                 set(CUDA_cupti_LIBRARY "${CUDA_SOURCE_DIR}/extras/CUPTI/lib64/libcupti_static.a")

                 elseif(EXISTS ${CUDA_SOURCE_DIR}/lib64/libcupti.so) 
        

        
          
                   set(CUDA_cupti_LIBRARY "${CUDA_SOURCE_DIR}/lib64/libcupti.so")

however, the transformations on train and test data might be different thus using this as an additional argument to pass different transforms for the test, train, and validation datasets be helpful and hassle-free.
Motivation
As I generally write a custom dataset class for loading in my image data it would be helpful and hassle-free if I could have an
option of using random_split() with this custom class and as an additional argument to this adding different transformations for train, test, and validation would be helpful.
Pitch
Depending on the split of data providing an option to treat the transformations separately for each of the split.
Alternatives
I  don't have an alternative for this, as the random_split function although being helpful does not accept the different transformations for my data.
Additional context
Thanks!

Hi,
My initial objective is simple; I would like to computes ConvTranspose2d with Conv2d layer (don't ask why please :D), and I succeed, but in an unexpected way.
The unexpected think in the code below is the use of transposeConv2dKernel()
function to "pre transpose" the conv2d W.
I really though that only Input Striding + Zero padding see inputStridedPadded  below would functionally match the ConvTransPose2d but this is still not functionally equivalent. I needed to transpose the conv2d Kernel W with transposeConv2dKernel()
to perform a 2d rotation, to exactly match.
This show that the course of conv2d is not equivalent to the course of ConvTransPose2d so i though it was.
I don't see the course of layers conv2d / transposeConv2dKernel in the doc, so could you give me the exact spec  please ?
See code below.
    k = 3
    len = 4
    stride = 3
    h, w = len, len
    n, m = 2, 2
    N = 1
    W = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=(n, m, k, k)).astype(np.float32)

    def rot2d180(a):
            a= np.rot90(a)
            a= np.rot90(a)
            return a

    def transposeConv2dKernel(a):
        a = np.moveaxis(a, [0,1, 2, 3], [1, 0, 2,3])
        for i in range(a.shape[0]):
            for j in range(a.shape[1]):
                a[i,j,::]  = rot2d180(a[i,j,::] )
        return a

    class tconv(torch.nn.Module):
        def create_convTranspose2d(self):
            layers = nn.ModuleList()
            C2D = nn.ConvTranspose2d(
                n, m, kernel_size=k, stride=stride, dilation=1, bias=False, output_padding=0, groups=1)
            C2D.weight.data = torch.tensor(W, requires_grad=False)
            layers.append(C2D)
            return torch.nn.Sequential(*layers)

        def __init__(self):
            super(tconv, self).__init__()
            self.layers = self.create_convTranspose2d()

        def forward(self, x):
            return self.layers(x)



    class tconvWithConv(torch.nn.Module):
        def create_conv2d(self):
            layers = nn.ModuleList()
            C2D = nn.Conv2d(
                n, m, kernel_size=k, stride=1, dilation=1, bias=False)
            W_ = transposeConv2dKernel(W)
            C2D.weight.data = torch.tensor(W_, requires_grad=False)
            layers.append(C2D)
            return torch.nn.Sequential(*layers)

        def __init__(self):
            super(tconvWithConv, self).__init__()
            self.layers = self.create_conv2d()

        def forward(self, x):
            return self.layers(x)


    # input
    input = np.random.randn(N, n, h, w) * 1

    # stride, padd input
    hi = (h - 1) * stride + 1 + 2 * (k - 1)
    wi = (w - 1) * stride + 1 + 2 * (k - 1)
    inputStridedPadded = np.zeros(shape=(N, n, hi, wi))
    rh = np.arange(start=k - 1, step=stride, stop=(hi) - (k - 1))
    rw = np.arange(start=k - 1, step=stride, stop=(wi) - (k - 1))
    xv, yv = np.meshgrid(rh, rw)
    inputStridedPadded[:, :, yv, xv] = input[:, :, ::]

    oTconv =  tconv().forward(torch.tensor(input).float()).detach().numpy()
    oTconvWconv = tconvWithConv().forward(torch.tensor(inputStridedPadded).float()).detach().numpy()

FFT tests start to fail in numpy>=1.20.1 on CPU and CUDA.
In particular we've isolated these failing tests:
test_reference_nd_fft_ifftn_cuda_complex64 (__main__.TestFFTCUDA)
test_reference_nd_fft_ifftn_cuda_float32 (__main__.TestFFTCUDA)
test_reference_nd_fft_irfftn_cuda_complex64 (__main__.TestFFTCUDA)
test_reference_nd_fft_irfftn_cuda_float32 (__main__.TestFFTCUDA)
which fail with small numerical errors:
AssertionError: False is not true : Scalars failed to compare as equal! Comparing the real part -0.5864181518554688 and -0.5864326355324252 gives a difference of 1.4483676956444924e-05, but the allowed difference with rtol=1.3e-06 and atol=1e-05 is only 1.0762362426192154e-05!
using numpy>=1.20.1, while numpy==1.19.2 lets these tests pass.
Note that the corresponding CPU tests also fail using the newer numpy version and work in the older one.
To Reproduce
Install numpy==1.20.1 and run:
python test_spectral_ops.py -v -k test_reference_nd_fft_ifftn_cpu_complex64

======================================================================
FAIL: test_reference_nd_fft_ifftn_cpu_complex64 (__main__.TestFFTCPU)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
[...]
AssertionError: False is not true : Scalars failed to compare as equal! Comparing the imaginary part 1.1501693725585938 and 1.1501473133785112 gives a difference of 2.2059180082578678e-05, but the allowed difference with rtol=1.3e-06 and atol=1e-05 is only 1.1495191507392065e-05!
We are currently unsure about the root cause, as nothing obvious points to this behavior in the numpy release notes.
We thought that a wrong dtype might be used:
The deprecation of numeric style type-codes np.dtype("Complex64") (with upper case spelling), is expired. "Complex64" corresponded to "complex128" and "Complex32" corresponded to "complex64".

but couldn't narrow it down to this usage so far.
We reproduced it on two different machines with source builds as well as the 1.8.1 binary and confirmed that numpy==1.19.2 lets the test pass, while numpy==1.20.1 fails it.
Let me know, if you need more information and a reproduction would be appreciated to confirm it on other machines.

🐛 Bug: The following is valid syntax but throws an error:
import torch
cu = torch.jit.CompilationUnit('''
def broadcast(a: List[int], b: List[int]):
output_size: List[int] = []
output_size.append(a[0] + (2 * b[d - 2]) - 4) // b[d - 2] + 1)
''')

type.present()INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "../torch/csrc/jit/frontend/parser.cpp":532, please report a bug to PyTorch.

I ran into this in symbolic shape analysis.
cc @gmagogsfm

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
The functions eig, eigh, svd and their derivatives present several problems.

eig is not always well-defined (only when the matrix is diagonalisable)
The eigen / singular vectors are not well-defined (if v is an eigen / singular vector, -v  is also an eigen / singular vector). Even more, when they have repeated eigen / singular values, the derivatives are not well defined (see #47599 (comment))

On the other hand, the eigenvalues / singular values of a matrix are always well-defined, and so are their derivatives when the eigenvalues / singular vectors are not used in the loss function.
As such, I see these functions as safer versions of the full factorisations, and should be preferred when possible. I believe we should support differentiability for these.
We could do so via a flag or, even better, detecting whether we are in a differentiable setting (if this is possible, I am not completely sure).
cc @ezyang @albanD @zou3519 @gqchen @pearu @nikitaved @soulitzer @jianyuh @mruberry @heitorschueroff @walterddr @IvanYashchuk @xwang233

🚀 Feature
The current implementation of torch.clip / torch.clamp only accepts scalars for min and max arguments. However, the NumPy versions of these functions support ndarray arguments for min and max when broadcastable with the input tensor.
The underlying implementation mimics torch.min(torch.max(x, max_limit), min_limit), which supports broadcasting, so it would nice if torch.clip and torch.clamp supported this as well.
Use Case
Consider an input tensor x of shape ... x d, where d is the dimension of the input (x can be thought of as a batched input). Every dimension i in {1 ,2 ... d} has it's own bound constraint (l_i <= x_i <= u_i). To project this batched input to a feasible set defined by the bound constraints (a box in d dimensions), we could use the torch.clip functionality as torch.clip(x, min=lower_bounds, max=upper_bounds), where lower_bounds and upper_bounds are d length vectors.
cc @mruberry @rgommers @heitorschueroff

🚀 Feature

Let RNNBase.reset_parameters and RNNCellBase.reset_parameters handle hidden_size = 0. Currently, they contain the line
stdv = 1.0 / math.sqrt(self.hidden_size)
which causes a ZeroDivisionError:
import torch

i_size = 10
h_size = 0
cell = torch.nn.GRUCell(i_size, h_size)

i = torch.rand(32, i_size)
h = torch.rand(32, h_size)
h_next = cell(i, h)
(Note that letting i_size = 0 instead works fine.)
Motivation

See #48152.
Example: Hyperparameters of a PODMP policy. Markovian (memoryless) policies are subsumed by h_size = 0. No additional refactoring or special casing required.
Pitch

Change the above to something like
stdv = 1 / math.sqrt(self.hidden_size) if self.hidden_size > 0 else 0
as was done in #56505.
cc @zou3519

🐛 Bug
Pytorch computes the derivative of torch.sinc(x) at x=0 to be NaN. Usually the derivative of sinc is considered 0 at x=0. See e.g. wolfram alpha, or it can be found via L'Hôpital's rule.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
>>> import torch
>>> x = torch.Tensor([0])
>>> x.requires_grad = True
>>> y = torch.sinc(x)
>>> y.backward()
>>> print(x.grad)
tensor([nan])
Expected behavior
I would expect the derivative to be computed as 0:
>>> import torch
>>> x = torch.Tensor([0])
>>> x.requires_grad = True
>>> y = torch.sinc(x)
>>> y.backward()
>>> print(x.grad)
tensor([0.])
Why?
The sinc function is critical for creating butterworth filters used heavily in digital signal processing. My network builds filters based on predicted passbands, but it fails to train because the derivative comes out as NaN.
